title: Encoding universal quantum computation into quantized Berry phases: Hardness results and classical algorithms
abstract: The Berry phase is a fundamental geometric quantity for characterizing the geometry and topology of quantum many-body systems. Previous work established a super-polynomial quantum advantage in Berry phase estimation at inverse-polynomial precision, given an ansatz state approximating the initial ground state. However, whether this hardness persists for Berry phases quantized by symmetry, which can be distinguished at constant precision, remained open. In this work, we characterize the computational complexity of quantized Berry phase estimation. First, we prove that deciding whether the Berry phase is exactly $0$ or $π$ is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete when the spectral gap is inverse-polynomially small. This result implies that distinguishing the quantized Berry phase still has a super-polynomial quantum advantage, assuming $\mathsf{BPP}\neq \mathsf{BQP}$. To prove this result, we introduce an encoding that maps the output of any quantum computation to a Berry phase that is exactly $0$ or $π$. Second, we extend this hardness to physically motivated Hamiltonians on a 2D square lattice, including Heisenberg and XY interactions. Third, we provide a classical polynomial-time algorithm for geometrically local Hamiltonians on fixed-dimensional lattices with constant spectral gaps. Therefore we identify that the spectral gap is a key resource for the classical tractability, rather than precision. These results establish a super-polynomial quantum advantage for computing a quantized topological invariant that is unchanged under symmetry- and gap-preserving deformations, and provide new steps towards practical quantum advantage in quantum physics.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the computational complexity of measuring quantized Berry phases in quantum many-body systems. It demonstrates that for systems with small spectral gaps, this measurement is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete, implying a quantum advantage. Conversely, it identifies the spectral gap as the critical resource, showing that constant gaps allow for efficient classical algorithms.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the computational complexity of estimating quantized Berry phases, specifically determining if the phase is exactly 0 or $\pi$.
main_result: It proves that distinguishing between $	heta_B=0$ and $	heta_B=\pi$ is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete for certain Hamiltonians, establishing a super-polynomial quantum advantage. However, it also shows that classical tractability is achieved when the spectral gap is constant.
method: The authors use quantum computation encoding to map the output of an arbitrary quantum circuit onto the Berry phase, allowing the use of established complexity theory tools.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum many-body systems described by local Hamiltonians on lattices (e.g., 2D square lattice with Heisenberg/XY interactions). The complexity is analyzed based on the spectral gap ($\Delta$) of the system.
key_observables: Quantized Berry Phase ($	heta_B$), Spectral Gap ($\Delta$), Acceptance Probability ($p_{acc}$)
important_parameters: Inverse-polynomial spectral gap, constant spectral gap, fidelity of the guiding state ($\gamma$)
main_assumptions: The hardness results assume an inverse-polynomially small spectral gap; classical tractability is shown under the assumption of a constant spectral gap.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the hardness mechanism by mapping computation acceptance probability to $	heta_B \in \{0, \pi\}$, shows the role of reflection symmetry in quantization, and summarizes the three main complexity results.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the hardness of the problem by encoding quantum computation into the Berry phase. It then extends this hardness to physically relevant 2D lattice models. Finally, it provides a constructive classical polynomial-time algorithm for the case where the spectral gap is constant.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the boundary between quantum computational advantage and classical simulation feasibility in fundamental quantum physics observables, which is central to quantum information theory applied to condensed matter.

The acceptance probability pacc of the encoded quantum computation is mapped to an effective two-level Hamiltonian in the low-energy subspace. In the YES case, pacc ≈1 and the loop encloses the origin, giving θB = π, whereas in the NO case, pacc ≈0 and the loop does not enclose it, giving θB = 0. The symmetry RH(θ)R† = H(−θ) quantizes the Berry phase of the full Hamiltonian to 0 or π. (b) The reflection R exchanges the two halves of the lattice and realizes the symmetry RH(θ)R† = H(−θ), which protects the quantization of the Berry phase throughout the reduction.
